# Exact three-interval depth and a common-parallel-flow obstruction

Even adding the same centrally symmetric continuous segment to every fiber
does NOT make maximum normalized mixed depth quasiconcave. The following
exact one-parameter family has a strict interior minimum. All three fibers
remain positive dimensional throughout the counterexample interval.

## 1. Complete depth formula for three symmetric interval fibers

Let a>0 and b>=a, and let

 S_(a,b)=({-1}x[0,a]) union ({0}x[0,b]) union ({1}x[0,a]).

It is induced by the convex body which is the convex hull of those three
intervals. The middle fiber is exactly [0,b], since [0,a] subset [0,b].
The total mixed measure is M=b+2a, using one-dimensional Lebesgue measure
on each fiber, equivalently H_1 on their union. Write F(a,b) for the maximum
normalized depth over actual points of S_(a,b). Then

 F(a,b)= (b+5a)/[4(b+2a)],       a<=b<=3a;
         (b+a)/[2(b+2a)],       b>=3a.             (1)

The unique maximizing point is in the middle fiber, with height

 x_*=(b+a)/4,  a<=b<=3a;
     (b-a)/2,  b>=3a.                             (2)

The formulas agree at b=3a. In particular F(a,a)=1/2, F(a,3a)=2/5,
and F(a,b) tends to 1/2 as b/a tends to infinity. The UNIQUE minimum
over ratios b/a>=1 is 2/5, at b/a=3.

## 2. Every oblique slope, explicitly

For x in the middle interval, define the clamp

    c_a(t)=max(0,min(a,t)).

A downward cap whose boundary passes through (0,x) has the form

    H_v^-={(z,X): X<=x+vz},

and its exact unnormalized mass is

    x+c_a(x+v)+c_a(x-v).                            (3)

For every x>=0,

    inf_(v in R) [c_a(x+v)+c_a(x-v)]=min(2x,a).     (4)

If 0<=x<=a/2, then either both clamped arguments are interior, giving
sum 2x, or clipping at zero raises the other argument to at least 2x,
or clipping at a gives a>=2x. Equality is attained at v=0. If x>=a/2,
both interior arguments sum to 2x>=a; one argument at least a gives
the same lower bound; if one is nonpositive, the other is at least
2x>=a. Equality a is attained by taking |v| sufficiently large that
one endpoint fiber is wholly contained and the other has zero length
in the cap. This also proves (4) when x>=a.

An upward cap through (0,x) has own-middle length b-x and endpoint sum
c_a(a-x+v)+c_a(a-x-v). If x>=a its infimum is zero, attained at v=0.
Otherwise apply (4) to a-x. Consequently the exact infima over the
two nonvertical orientations are

    L(x)=x+min(2x,a),
    U(x)=b-x+min(2(a-x)_+,a).                       (5)

Every infimum just used is attained at a finite slope; no limiting vertical
halfspace is being substituted for an oblique one. Hyperplane boundaries
within each positive-length fiber have zero H_1 measure.

The vertical closed halfspaces through (0,x) have mass b+a. A vertical
halfspace containing that point contains at least one such through-point
halfspace, so cannot have smaller mass. The values in (5) are at most
b+a. Every nonvertical containing halfspace similarly contains the parallel
one through (0,x). It follows that the exact depth there is

    depth_(S_(a,b))(0,x)=min(L(x),U(x))/(b+2a).      (6)

This accounts for EVERY closed ambient halfspace, including the vertical
ones carrying the entire middle fiber on their boundary.

The functions L and U are respectively strictly increasing and strictly
decreasing on [0,b]. Their unique intersection therefore maximizes (6).
For clarity their pieces are

 L(x)=3x for x<=a/2, and x+a for x>=a/2;

 U(x)=b+a-x for 0<=x<=a/2,
      b+2a-3x for a/2<=x<=a,
      b-x for a<=x<=b.

Since b>=a, the intersection is at least a/2. If b<=3a it lies between
a/2 and a and solves x+a=b+2a-3x, giving the first formulas (1)--(2).
If b>=3a it lies at least a and solves x+a=b-x, giving the second ones.

No endpoint fiber supplies a larger maximum. At either extreme index,
an own-fiber cap can be extended with a sufficiently large integer tilt
to exclude the other two compact fibers. Thus a point at height x in an
endpoint interval has mixed depth at most min(x,a-x)/M<=a/(2M).
Conversely every containing cap captures at least that much from its own
fiber, so this endpoint bound is exact. The middle maximum in (1) has
absolute mass at least 3a/2, strictly larger. This proves the asserted
unique global maximizer as well as the formulas.

Lastly, in the first branch the derivative with respect to r=b/a of
(r+5)/[4(r+2)] is -3/[4(r+2)^2]<0. In the second branch the derivative
of (r+1)/[2(r+2)] is 1/[2(r+2)^2]>0. This proves the exact minimum claim.

## 3. A common centrally symmetric addend produces the dip

Let C_0 in R x R be the convex hull of

    {-1}x[0,1], {0}x[0,5], {1}x[0,1].

Equivalently C_0 has lower boundary zero and upper boundary 5-4|z|
on -1<=z<=1. Let L=[-1,1] in the continuous coordinate and define

    C_t=C_0+({0}x tL), t>=0.

These are actual convex bodies. Their integer projection remains exactly
{-1,0,1}, and their fibers are

    [-t,1+t], [-t,5+t], [-t,1+t].                  (7)

Every fiber center stays fixed, while every length increases by exactly
2t. Translating the continuous coordinate by t preserves the lattice,
halfspaces, and measure and turns (7) into S_(a,b) with

    a=1+2t, b=5+2t.

Thus the maximum normalized mixed depth is EXACTLY

    F_t=(3+2t)/(7+6t),          0<=t<=1/2;
        (5+6t)/[2(7+6t)],      t>=1/2.             (8)

The maximizing points in the original coordinates are respectively

    (0,2-t), 0<=t<=1/2;
    (0,3/2), t>=1/2.

The first branch of (8) decreases strictly, and the second increases
strictly. At the three rational parameters

    F_0=3/7, F_(1/2)=2/5, F_3=23/50,

one has

    F_(1/2)=2/5<min(3/7,23/50)=3/7.               (9)

Since 1/2=(5/6)0+(1/6)3, (9) directly contradicts quasiconcavity on
[0,3]. It also rules out either monotonicity direction on the whole
outer-parallel flow. The counterexample uses a fixed symmetric L, a fixed
integer projection, constant fiber centers, and positive interval fibers
at every parameter under consideration.

## 4. Inner erosions and degenerate limits

For -1/2<=t<0, the same fiber formula (7) is the valid vertical erosion

    {w: w+({0}x[-s,s]) subset C_0},  s=-t.

Explicitly its fibers are
[s,5-4|z|-s]. The projection remains [-1,1] as long as s<=1/2.
Thus (8)'s first branch also holds on [-1/2,0), using the same translation.
At t=-1/2 the endpoint fibers are singleton points of zero H_1 mass;
the middle interval still has positive length four. The maximum depth is
then 1/2 at its midpoint, agreeing with the limit of (8). The body itself
is still two-dimensional. Larger erosions change the integer projection
and are not needed for this statement.

More generally (1)'s second branch extends to a=0,b>0: only the middle
fiber contributes H_1 measure, and its unique deepest point is b/2 with
depth 1/2. If a=b=0 then the displayed normalization has zero H_1 mass
and the induced ambient convex hull is not a two-dimensional convex body;
that case is excluded rather than assigned the wrong measure. For b<a
the proposed three intervals are not convex-compatible: the actual middle
fiber of their convex hull enlarges to [0,a]. This explains the hypothesis
b>=a and is not a hidden restriction on the flow counterexample.

The result concerns a deformation strategy. It supplies no counterexample
to OC; its minimum 2/5 is itself strictly larger than the n=d=1 OC bound
1/4. No conclusion about different continuous addends or a corrected flow
invariant is implied.

## 5. The TRUE centroid throughout this family

The actual mixed-volume centroid has integer base zero for every a,b,
because the endpoint volumes agree. If r=b/a>=1, its height divided by a is

    c(r)=(r^2+2)/[2(r+2)].

Substituting this actual centroid into the exact all-slope formula (6)
gives its normalized depth

 (r^2+2r+6)/[2(r+2)^2],       1<=r<=2 and 4<=r;
 (-r^2+8r+2)/[2(r+2)^2],      2<=r<=1+sqrt(3);
 (r^2+4r-2)/[2(r+2)^2],       1+sqrt(3)<=r<=4.       (10)

Indeed c(r)>=1/2, it crosses height one at r=1+sqrt(3), and its difference
from the optimal height in (2) has the sign of (r-1)(r-2) for r<=3,
and the sign of 4-r for r>=3. These facts identify which piece of (5)
is smaller and give (10). The derivatives of the three rational expressions
in their displayed order are respectively

    (r-4)/(r+2)^3, 6(1-r)/(r+2)^3, 6/(r+2)^3.

Therefore the TRUE centroid depth has its unique global minimum at
r=1+sqrt(3), with value (sqrt(3)-1)/2. This restricted true-centroid family
satisfies a bound strictly stronger than the n=d=1 OC constant 1/4. It
does not imply the conditional-centroid assertion for arbitrary interval
families, or for any higher continuous dimension.
